title: not charity
hook: not charity — justice; the box on the counter
carry: give before you feel like it
tomorrow: the story every Passover retells in first person

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jacob, wrestling till dawn, limping, renamed Israel. Your line was you'll limp and you'll be blessed. Did something hard give you anything back? Day ten.

On the counter in some Jewish kitchens sits a small tin box with a slot in the top. Nobody makes a speech about it. A kid drops in a coin after finding one on the sidewalk. A grandmother drops a few in on Friday afternoon, before she lights the candles. When it's full, it goes to a food bank, a school, a family down the street. It's easy to call that charity. But the word written on the box doesn't mean charity. It means something sharper. Today: the box on the counter, and why it isn't a favor.
screen: `A TIN BOX WITH A SLOT.` → `COINS BEFORE THE CANDLES.` → `IT ISN'T CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Tzedakah comes from tzedek: justice, righteousness, what's right. Charity, in English, sounds like a kindness you choose when you feel moved to. Tzedakah assumes something else: that part of what you have was never fully yours. It's the poor person's share, and giving it is setting things right. That's why, in Jewish law, it isn't optional. The Talmud says that even someone who lives on tzedakah should give some. Deuteronomy says: "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." The word there is tzedek, said twice. The rabbis asked why twice, and one answer is: pursue justice, and pursue it justly, even in how you give. The legal scholar Maimonides laid out eight levels of tzedakah, like the rungs of a ladder. Near the bottom: giving, but grudgingly. Higher: giving before you're asked. Higher still: giving so that neither side knows the other, so nobody has to feel ashamed. And the top rung, above all the others: helping someone so they won't need help again. A loan, a partnership, a job. Tzedakah at its best ends the need for tzedakah. Maimonides also made an observation about habit. A person who gives a thousand coins at once, he said, grows less than a person who gives one coin a thousand times, because it's the repeated act that shapes the giver. That's what the box on the counter is for. Not a feeling of generosity, waited for. A habit, built one coin at a time, until justice is just something your hands do.
screen: `TZEDEK — JUSTICE, NOT CHARITY.` · `EVEN THE POOR GIVE.` · `EIGHT RUNGS OF A LADDER.` · `ONE COIN, A THOUSAND TIMES.` · then, large: `JUSTICE, JUSTICE SHALT THOU FOLLOW.`

segments.voice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Think of one need near you: a food bank, a neighbor, a cause you've meant to support. Decide on one small, specific amount, of money or of time. Not what feels generous. Just what's fair. Hold that decision until the bell ends, and then act on it before the feeling fades. The bell holds the time.
Tzedakah. Giving as justice, the poor person's share, not a favor. Tenth word.
Your line: give before you feel like it. Today, give one small thing, a coin, a donation, an hour, before you've talked yourself into it or out of it. Day ten.

screen: `DAY 10 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE STORY EVERY PASSOVER RETELLS IN FIRST PERSON.`

howItsDone: Some Jewish homes keep a tzedakah box, and some families drop coins in before lighting Shabbat candles; traditional Jewish law expects everyone to give, and some give a tenth of their income (ma'aser).

fork.setup: you have a thousand coins to give this year. by Maimonides' teaching, which grows you more as a giver?
options: one gift of a thousand coins.
one coin, given a thousand times.
fork.reveal: one coin, a thousand times: the repeated act shapes the person. that's the box on the counter.

original.note: Hebrew: from tzedek, justice or righteousness.

trapdoor: what it means: justice. giving back the share that belongs to the poor, expected of everyone.
what a scholar hears: Maimonides' eight levels (Gifts to the Poor, chapter 10) put self-sufficiency at the top, and his comment on Avot prefers a thousand small gifts to one large one.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 7b (even one who lives on tzedakah gives)
